problems.description: Test DB is a real file (test_todos.db) with manual os.remove cleanup rather than tmp_path fixture; a failed test can leave stale state and the cleanup is duplicated in fixture setup and teardown.
test_list_tasks_with_data asserts list ordering (data[0] == 'Task 2') which couples the test to the current insertion-order implementation rather than asserting on task fields independent of order.
No coverage of update validation (e.g. empty/invalid status values) or the task-not-found error handling on POST/PUT beyond 404, leaving validation paths untested.
Cognitive complexity +11 mostly accumulates from repetitive three-way title validation (empty vs whitespace vs missing); consolidating into a parametrized test would reduce duplication.

strengths: Test classes and snake_case test functions follow pytest conventions cleanly; none of the 12 reported convention violations are in the new file.
Comprehensive CRUD coverage including both success and failure paths (404, missing/empty/whitespace title) with explicit status-code assertions.
Autouse fixture isolates each test against a clean database, preventing cross-test pollution.
Error-message assertions pin the API contract (e.g. 'title is required', 'task not found') which guards against regressions in the app's error responses.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-structured pytest suite for the task API with solid CRUD and error-path coverage, and the low convention score is attributable to pre-existing files (app.py, celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, __init__.py) untouched by this commit.

problems.description: migrate() re-declares the users table schema already defined in init_db(), creating two sources of truth for the schema and an inconsistent migration path (users table is only created as a side effect of tasks lacking owner_id).
SECRET_KEY falls back to a hard-coded 'dev-secret-change-me' default in the production code path; a misconfigured deployment silently signs/validates tokens with a known key.
datetime.utcnow() is deprecated since Python 3.12; should use datetime.now(timezone.utc).

New/affected files (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, __init__.py) introduce naming violations — snake_case functions/classes and module constants not in UPPER_CASE — which drive the convention score to 0.73.
Migration and fresh-init paths diverge: init_db() creates both tables on new DBs, while migrate() only patches legacy DBs, making schema evolution ad-hoc rather than versioned.

strengths: Passwords are hashed via werkzeug (never stored plaintext), and tokens expire after 24h.
All task queries (get_tasks, get_task, update_task) are owner-scoped, preventing horizontal cross-user access.
Auth layer is woven into the existing single-file structure using established helpers (get_db, jsonify, section headers), respecting the seed's seams.
Clean decorator-based route protection with consistent 401 responses for missing, expired, and invalid tokens.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, security-conscious JWT auth feature that respects the single-file architecture and owner-scopes every query, though the ad-hoc migrate() duplicate-schema logic and naming drift in celery_config/celery_tasks/__init__ introduce technical debt.

problems.description: send_notification_email task is a stub that only prints — no email is actually sent, so the feature is non-functional infrastructure.
Top-level 'from celery_tasks import send_notification_email' in app.py forces celery/redis to be installed for the app to boot at all, tightly coupling the whole app to a side-effect subsystem.
Hardcoded 'redis://localhost:6379/0' broker/backend in celery_config.py; not env-driven, so deployments/config variance are not supported.
Fabricated fallback email f"{username}@example.com" ships fake addresses when a user has no email, which would send to non-existent mailboxes.
Module-level config constants (broker_url, result_backend) in celery_config.py should be UPPER_CASE per PEP8.
Tests verify the delay call fires/doesn't fire but never assert the email address passed, nor the email-column migration path (ALTER TABLE), nor the fallback-address logic.

strengths: Correct transition detection — notification only fires on a genuine status change to 'completed', not on repeat or unrelated title edits.
Defensive migration using PRAGMA column check plus ALTER TABLE to handle pre-existing databases.
Strong test coverage of the trigger edge cases with proper mock patching of .delay.
Clean separation of the Celery app and config into dedicated modules rather than inlining in app.py.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid structure and edge-case handling, but ships a print-only stub behind a heavy new Celery/Redis dependency and a fabricated fallback email, so it's a wash — technically neater, functionally incomplete.

problems.description: BaseRepository forces a generic create/find_by_id abstract contract on every repository via *args/**kwargs, but the two repositories have genuinely different shapes (TaskRepository needs find_all_by_owner, UserRepository needs find_by_username and returns None on create conflict). The base class adds coupling without a real shared contract.
Repositories are instantiated as module-level singletons (task_repo = TaskRepository(get_db)) at import time, baking the Flask connection factory in and making the repos harder to test in isolation.
The refactor extracts three new classes (+3 classes) but adds no tests for the repository layer; behavior is only covered transitively through route tests.

Abstract method signatures use *args/**kwargs with ellipsis bodies and the new public methods lack type hints, weakening the API contract the abstraction claims to provide (cognitive complexity +3 per SonarQube).

Convention score is 0.73 with 12 flagged violations, but most (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, __init__.py) are in files untouched by this commit and appear pre-existing; the new repositories themselves are not among the flagged offenders.

strengths: Consolidates scattered SQL in route handlers into focused TaskRepository/UserRepository classes, removing duplicated connection handling.
SonarQube shows 3 smells removed with zero new bugs and no duplication, so the refactor is net-clean by static analysis.
Route handlers keep identical responses and status codes; the public API contract is unchanged (pure behavior-preserving extraction).
Naming maps cleanly to usage (create, find_by_id, find_all_by_owner, find_by_username) matching the pre-existing route semantics.
commit_reviews.summary: A behavior-preserving repository extraction that cleans up the data layer (smells -3) and matches existing module conventions, held back only by a forced generic abstract base, import-time singletons, and missing tests for the new layer.

problems.description: Limiter is instantiated and limiter.init_app(app) runs at module import with storage_uri pinned to REDIS_URL; without a reachable Redis the app stalls up to the 30s socket_connect_timeout on the first rate-limited request instead of degrading gracefully.
GET /tasks response shape changes from a bare list to an envelope dict (data/next_cursor/total) — a breaking change for existing API consumers.
next_cursor is emitted whenever exactly `limit` rows are returned, even when no further pages exist, producing a trailing empty page on the final request.

Discrepancy flagged: the measured convention score (0.73, 12 violations) is dominated by pre-existing violations in celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, and __init__.py — files untouched by this commit; the commit's own additions follow snake_case/PascalCase correctly.
Cognitive complexity delta of +91 suggests the rate-limit keying wiring (JWT decode plus IP fallback branches) could be extracted into a dedicated module to keep app.py readable.

strengths: Cursor-based keyset pagination implemented in the repository layer (WHERE id < ? ORDER BY id DESC), consistent with the existing BaseRepository pattern and index-friendly.
Per-user rate limiting keyed off the JWT with IP fallback, env-configurable defaults (REDIS_URL, RATE_LIMIT), and a dedicated 429 handler exposing Retry-After.
Comprehensive tests for rate limiting and pagination, including limiter.reset() fixture hygiene and input clamping (limit clamped to 1..100).
No new bugs, two smells fixed, zero duplication introduced per SonarQube.
commit_reviews.summary: Well-tested feature work that respects the existing repository and app-layer patterns and ships with no new bugs, though it introduces a breaking API envelope change and a module-import-time Redis coupling; the low convention score is mostly pre-existing debt in files this commit never touched.

compounding_issues: SECRET_KEY hardcoded default 'dev-secret-change-me' introduced in S1 (JWT auth) and never replaced through S5 — security debt carried across every session
Celery imported at module load in app.py (S3) made the broker a hard runtime dependency of the core app rather than an isolated integration seam
S3 notification logic references a synthetic email fallback (username@example.com), a leaky placeholder that S4's refactor preserved verbatim
S1's owner_id FK on tasks was added via an ALTER TABLE migration path, and S2/S3 stacked more column additions onto the same ad-hoc migrate() — schema evolution grew fragile but never consolidated
key_decisions: S1: Adopt JWT auth with per-owner task scoping (owner_id FK) as the security model every later session built on
S1: Build an ad-hoc migrate() helper, enabling incremental schema evolution (email, owner_id) across sessions
S3: Introduce Celery/Redis for async completion notifications — a broker dependency layered into a minimal tier-1 app
S4: Extract repositories/ package (base/task/user) and slim app.py from inline SQL to repo calls — the pivotal structural refactor
S5: Add Redis-backed Flask-Limiter with a JWT-aware key function plus cursor-based pagination in the repository layer
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality rose steadily and then accelerated. Session 1 established a sound foundation (auth, ownership, migration) and test discipline (12 tests); Session 2 added a coherent feature (email + async notification) on that base. Session 3 integrated Celery cleanly with tests growing to 32, though it cemented a broker dependency into app.py. The sharpest inflection came in Session 4's refactor, which extracted a repository layer and cut app.py's inline data access, leaving a much cleaner surface for Session 5's cross-cutting additions (rate limiting, pagination). Session 5 landed cleanly on the refactored structure with tests reaching 43, demonstrating that early structural decisions paid off. The only consistent drag was the never-replaced dev SECRET_KEY and the creeping external dependencies (Celery, Redis) that the 5-session arc accumulated without consolidation.
story_review.summary: A textbook coherent multi-session arc — greenfield, feature, integration, refactor, cross-cutting — where early security/scoping decisions compounded favorably and quality improved monotonically, marred only by a persistent dev-secret default and unreconciled broker dependencies.
